summary.text: Write \(\binom{k p^r}{p^r}=k\prod_{s=1}^r T_s(k)\), where \(T_s(k)\) is a product over the residues below \(p^s\) not divisible by \(p\), and pair each residue \(i\) with \(p^s-i\) to obtain a quadratic \(p\)-adic expansion. Unit-group symmetry supplies the needed divisibility of the reciprocal-square sums (while for \(r=2\) the reciprocal-fourth-power remainder gains an extra factor of \(p\) from its \(p\) identical residue blocks), so higher terms vanish modulo \(p^{3r+3}\) and the remaining linear terms for \(k=3\) and \(k=2\) cancel in the weighted combination.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
Fix a prime \(p\geq 3\) and an integer \(r\geq2\). We prove
\[
 a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]
Throughout the main part of the proof, all calculations take place in a residue ring
\[
 R_M=\mathbb Z/p^M\mathbb Z.
\]
Every integer not divisible by \(p\) is a unit in this ring, so fractions whose denominators are prime to \(p\) are legitimate. Saying that an element of \(R_M\) is divisible by \(p^e\) has its usual meaning. We will also repeatedly use the fact that \(p^M=0\) in \(R_M\).

For \(s\geq1\), write
\[
 I_s=\{i:0\leq i<p^s,\ p\nmid i\}.
\]
(The element \(0\) is automatically absent.) Define
\[
 h_{s,i}=\frac1{i(p^s-i)},\qquad
 H_s=\sum_{i\in I_s}h_{s,i}
\]
in whatever ring \(R_M\) is under consideration. Also, for a positive integer \(k\), define the level product
\[
 T_s(k)=\prod_{i\in I_s}\left(1-\frac{k p^s}{i}\right).
\]
Finally put
\[
 U_r(k)=\prod_{s=1}^r T_s(k),\qquad U_0(k)=1.
\]
We first establish the congruence estimates for these products.

### 1. Reciprocal-sum estimates

The reflection \(i\mapsto p^s-i\) permutes \(I_s\). On reducing modulo \(p^s\), we have
\[
 p^s-i\equiv-i,
\]
and hence
\[
 h_{s,i}=\frac1{i(p^s-i)}\equiv-\frac1{i^2}\pmod {p^s}.
\]
We claim that
\[
 3\sum_{i\in I_s}\frac1{i^2}\equiv0\pmod {p^s}.
\]
Indeed, \(I_s\) is a complete set of representatives for the units modulo \(p^s\). Inversion permutes those units, so the sum of their inverse squares equals the sum of their squares. Multiplication by \(2\) also permutes the units because \(p\geq3\). Therefore, if \(S\) denotes the sum of the squares of all units modulo \(p^s\), then
\[
 S=\sum_u(2u)^2=4S,
\]
so \(3S=0\). Consequently
\[
 3H_s\equiv0\pmod {p^s}.
\]
Equivalently, in every \(R_M\) with \(M\geq s\),
\[
 p^s\mid 3H_s. \tag{1}
\]
This formulation deliberately retains the factor \(3\), and therefore applies uniformly when \(p=3\).

We shall need one extra estimate at level \(s=2\):
\[
 p\mid\sum_{i\in I_2}h_{2,i}^{\,2}. \tag{2}
\]
To prove it, reduce modulo \(p\). Since \(p^2-i\equiv-i\pmod p\),
\[
 h_{2,i}^{\,2}\equiv i^{-4}\pmod p.
\]
As \(i\) runs from \(0\) to \(p^2-1\), every residue modulo \(p\) occurs exactly \(p\) times. Terms divisible by \(p\) may be included because their inverse is interpreted as zero after the restriction is removed, or, equivalently, one may simply count the nonzero residue classes. Thus
\[
 
 \sum_{i\in I_2}i^{-4}
 =p\sum_{x\in(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z)^\times}x^{-4}=0
\]
in \(\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z\), proving (2).

### 2. Two elementary product expansions

We use the following general facts in any commutative ring. Let \(f_i\) be a finite family, each divisible by an element \(d\), and set
\[
 P=\prod_i(1+f_i),\qquad S=\sum_i f_i,\qquad Q=\sum_i f_i^2.
\]
Then
\[
 d^2\mid P-1-S, \tag{3}
\]
and
\[
 d^3\mid 2(P-1-S)-S^2+Q. \tag{4}
\]
The first assertion follows by expanding the product: after the constant and linear terms are removed, every remaining monomial contains at least two of the \(f_i\). For the second, the quadratic part of \(P-1-S\) is \(\sum_{i<j}f_if_j\), while
\[
 S^2-Q=2\sum_{i<j}f_if_j.
\]
Thus the displayed combination has no terms of degree below three, and every remaining monomial is divisible by \(d^3\). This argument is denominator-free and remains valid when \(2\) or \(3\) is not invertible. Alternatively, both statements follow directly by induction on the number of factors.

We will also use the elementary weighted-product consequence: if \(d\mid c(F_i-1)\) for every factor \(F_i\), then
\[
 d\mid c\left(\prod_iF_i-1\right). \tag{5}
\]
Indeed, adding one factor uses
\[
 c(FG-1)=c(F-1)G+c(G-1),
\]
and induction proves the assertion.

### 3. Pairing the level products

Reflection preserves \(I_s\), and hence a second copy of \(T_s(k)\) can be indexed by \(p^s-i\). Pairing the corresponding factors gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\left(1-\frac{kp^s}{i}\right)
 \left(1-\frac{kp^s}{p^s-i}\right)\\
&\qquad=1+k(k-1)p^{2s}\frac1{i(p^s-i)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Therefore
\[
 T_s(k)^2
 =\prod_{i\in I_s}\left(1+k(k-1)p^{2s}h_{s,i}\right). \tag{6}
\]

Apply (3) to the right side with
\[
 f_i=k(k-1)p^{2s}h_{s,i},\qquad d=p^{2s}.
\]
The error after the linear term is divisible by \(p^{4s}\), hence by \(p^{3s}\). By (1), the linear sum satisfies
\[
 p^{3s}\mid 3\sum_i f_i,
\]
because it is \(k(k-1)p^{2s}H_s\). It follows from (6) that
\[
 p^{3s}\mid3\bigl(T_s(k)^2-1\bigr). \tag{7}
\]
Moreover, \(T_s(k)\equiv1\pmod p\), since every factor is congruent to \(1\) modulo \(p\). Thus
\[
 T_s(k)+1\equiv2\pmod p,
\]
which is a unit because \(p\) is odd. Factoring
\[
 T_s(k)^2-1=(T_s(k)-1)(T_s(k)+1)
\]
and cancelling this unit in (7), we obtain the important estimate
\[
 p^{3s}\mid3\bigl(T_s(k)-1\bigr). \tag{8}
\]

Applying (5) to \(U_m(k)=\prod_{s=1}^mT_s(k)\), and noting that \(3s\geq3\), gives
\[
 p^3\mid3\bigl(U_m(k)-1\bigr) \tag{9}
\]
whenever all calculations are made modulo a sufficiently high power of \(p\).

### 4. A sharper linearization of \(T_r(k)^2\)

We now work specifically in
\[
 R=\mathbb Z/p^{3r+3}\mathbb Z,
\]
where \(r\geq2\). Put
\[
 c=k(k-1),\qquad f_i=c p^{2r}h_{r,i},
\]
and let \(S=\sum_i f_i=c p^{2r}H_r\), \(Q=\sum_i f_i^2\). Equation (6) says
\[
 T_r(k)^2=\prod_i(1+f_i).
\]
We claim
\[
 9\left(T_r(k)^2-1-k(k-1)p^{2r}H_r\right)=0
 \quad\text{in }R. \tag{10}
\]

First, by (1), \(p^{3r}\mid3S\). Squaring shows that \(p^{6r}\mid9S^2\). Since
\[
 6r\geq3r+3

after \(r\geq1\), it follows that
\[
 9S^2=0\quad\text{in }R. \tag{11}
\]

Next we show \(Q=0\) in \(R\). If \(r\geq3\), every \(f_i^2\) contains \(p^{4r}\), and
\[
 4r\geq3r+3,
\]
so every summand is zero. The only remaining case is \(r=2\). Then
\[
 Q=c^2p^8\sum_{i\in I_2}h_{2,i}^{\,2}.
\]
By (2), the final sum is divisible by \(p\), so \(Q\) is divisible by \(p^9\). Here \(3r+3=9\), and again \(Q=0\) in \(R\). This is the sole special exponent case in the proof.

Now apply (4) with \(d=p^{2r}\). Its error is divisible by \(p^{6r}\), hence is zero in \(R\), and therefore
\[
 2\left(\prod_i(1+f_i)-1-S\right)-S^2+Q=0.
\]
Using \(Q=0\), multiplying by \(9\), and using (11), we get
\[
 18\left(\prod_i(1+f_i)-1-S\right)=0.
\]
Since \(2\) is a unit modulo \(p^{3r+3}\), it can be cancelled, giving exactly (10).

For the two values of \(k\) needed below, set
\[
 t=T_r(3),\qquad w=T_r(2),\qquad y=p^{2r}H_r.
\]
Then (10) becomes
\[
 9(t^2-1-6y)=0, \tag{12}
\]
\[
 9(w^2-1-2y)=0. \tag{13}
\]

### 5. Cancellation between the \(k=3\) and \(k=2\) products

Still in \(R=\mathbb Z/p^{3r+3}\mathbb Z\), put
\[
 u=U_{r-1}(3),\qquad v=U_{r-1}(2).
\]
By (9),
\[
 p^3\mid3(u-1),\qquad p^3\mid3(v-1). \tag{14}
\]
By (8), applied to \(w=T_r(2)\),
\[
 p^{3r}\mid3(w-1),

a fortiori
\[
 p^3\mid3(w-1). \tag{15}
\]
The identity
\[
 u^2(w+1)-2v
 =(u-1)(u+1)(w+1)+(w-1)-2(v-1)

together with (14) and (15) yields
\[
 p^3\mid3\bigl(u^2(w+1)-2v\bigr). \tag{16}
\]
On the other hand, (1) gives
\[
 p^{3r}\mid3y, \tag{17}
\]
because \(y=p^{2r}H_r\). Multiplying (16) and (17), and using
\[
 p^{3r}p^3=p^{3r+3}=0\quad\text{in }R,
\]
we obtain
\[
 9y\bigl(u^2(w+1)-2v\bigr)=0. \tag{18}
\]
In particular the same is true after multiplication by \(6\):
\[
 54y\bigl(u^2(w+1)-2v\bigr)=0. \tag{19}
\]

We now combine (12), (13), and (19). A direct algebraic expansion gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
&\Bigl(9u^2t^2-54vw-(9u^2-54v)\Bigr)(w+1)\\
&\quad=u^2(w+1)\,9(t^2-1-6y)
      -6v\,9(w^2-1-2y)\\
&\qquad\quad+54y\bigl(u^2(w+1)-2v\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]
Every term on the right is zero by (12), (13), and (19). Hence the left side is zero. But \(w\equiv1\pmod p\), so \(w+1\equiv2\pmod p\), and \(w+1\) is a unit. Cancelling it gives
\[
 9u^2t^2-54vw=9u^2-54v.
\]
Since
\[
 U_r(3)=U_{r-1}(3)T_r(3)=ut,
\qquad
 U_r(2)=U_{r-1}(2)T_r(2)=vw,
\]
we have proved
\[
 9U_r(3)^2-54U_r(2)
 =9U_{r-1}(3)^2-54U_{r-1}(2)
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p^{3r+3}\mathbb Z. \tag{20}
\]

### 6. Reconstruction of the binomial coefficients

It remains to connect the products \(U_r(k)\) to binomial coefficients. We prove that, for every positive integer \(k\),
\[
 \binom{kp^m}{p^m}=kU_m(k) \tag{21}
\]
in every residue ring \(R_M\).

We begin with an integer identity. If \(n\) is positive and odd, then
\[
 \binom{kn}{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}i
 =k\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(i-kn). \tag{22}
\]
Indeed, the standard factorial formula gives
\[
 \binom{kn}{n}\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}i
 =k\prod_{i=1}^{n-1}(kn-i).
\]
There are \(n-1\) factors, and \(n-1\) is even, so replacing every \(kn-i\) by \(-(i-kn)\) introduces no sign, proving (22).

Apply (22) with \(n=pm\), where \(p\) and \(m\) are odd, and separate in each product the indices divisible by \(p\). The multiples of \(p\) in \(1,\ldots,pm-1\) are exactly \(pj\) for \(1\leq j<m\). Thus
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^{pm-1}i
 =p^{m-1}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}j\right)
   \left(\prod_{\substack{1\leq i<pm\\p\nmid i}}i\right),

after understanding that the factors in the final product are the complementary, nonmultiples-of-\(p\) factors. Similarly,
\[
 \prod_{i=1}^{pm-1}(i-kpm)
 =p^{m-1}\left(\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}(j-km)\right)
   \left(\prod_{\substack{1\leq i<pm\\p\nmid i}}(i-kpm)\right).

after splitting the product into its divisible and nondivisible indices. Comparing (22) for \(pm\) with (22) for \(m\), and cancelling the common nonzero integer factor coming from the divisible indices, yields
\[
 \binom{kpm}{pm}
 \prod_{\substack{1\leq i<pm\\p\nmid i}}i
 =\binom{km}{m}
 \prod_{\substack{1\leq i<pm\\p\nmid i}}(i-kpm). \tag{23}
\]

Now take \(m=p^s\). Since \(p\geq3\), both \(p\) and \(p^s\) are odd, so (23) applies. Pass to \(R_M\). Every factor \(i\) in the displayed restricted product is a unit, so their product can be cancelled. We get
\[
\begin{aligned}
 \binom{kp^{s+1}}{p^{s+1}}
 &=\binom{kp^s}{p^s}
   \prod_{i\in I_{s+1}}\frac{i-kp^{s+1}}i\\
 &=\binom{kp^s}{p^s}T_{s+1}(k). \tag{24}
\end{aligned}
\]
At level zero, \(\binom{k}{1}=k\). Iterating (24) proves (21).

### 7. Conclusion

Use (21) in the ring \(R=\mathbb Z/p^{3r+3}\mathbb Z\). For every \(m\),
\[
 \binom{3p^m}{p^m}=3U_m(3),
 \qquad
 \binom{2p^m}{p^m}=2U_m(2).
\]
Consequently
\[
\begin{aligned}
 a(p^m)
 &=\binom{3p^m}{p^m}^2-27\binom{2p^m}{p^m}\\
 &=9U_m(3)^2-54U_m(2)
\end{aligned}
\]
in \(R\). Taking \(m=r\) and \(m=r-1\), equation (20) therefore says precisely that
\[
 a(p^r)=a(p^{r-1})
 \quad\text{in }\mathbb Z/p^{3r+3}\mathbb Z.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
 \boxed{a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}}.
\]
This holds for every prime \(p\geq3\) and every \(r\geq2\), as required.
